body:
Establishment of the Khalji Dynasty

The Khalji Dynasty ruled Delhi from 1290 to 1320. It succeeded the Mamluk Dynasty and marked an important phase in the territorial expansion of the Delhi Sultanate.

Jalaluddin Firuz Khalji (1290–1296) founded the dynasty in 1290. His reign was comparatively short and was mainly concerned with securing the new dynasty's position.

In 1296, Jalaluddin was killed by his nephew Alauddin Khalji, who then became Sultan. Alauddin's reign brought major military conquests and stronger efforts to control the army, revenue and markets.

Alauddin Khalji: Major conquests

Alauddin Khalji (1296–1316) was one of the most important expansionist rulers of the Delhi Sultanate. His campaigns extended Delhi's authority over large parts of northern, western and central India, while military expeditions reached the Deccan and southern India.

Gujarat: Conquest in 1299

One of Alauddin's most important early campaigns was the conquest of Gujarat in 1299.

The expedition was led by his commanders Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan. Sultanate forces attacked the region and sacked Anhilwara, also known as Anhilwad Patan, which was an important political centre of the Chaulukya-Vaghela kingdom.

Gujarat was attractive because of its commercial wealth and important trading connections. The conquest extended Delhi's authority into western India. Alp Khan was subsequently entrusted with its provincial administration.

Gujarat connection: Alauddin Khalji's Gujarat expedition occurred in 1299. The important political centre attacked was Anhilwara or Patan.

Conquests in Rajasthan and central India

Alauddin sought to control important forts, routes and regional kingdoms in Rajasthan and central India.

  • Ranthambore: Captured in 1301 after a prolonged struggle against its Chauhan ruler, Hammir Dev.
  • Chittor: Captured in 1303, extending Sultanate influence in Mewar.
  • Malwa: Conquered in 1305, extending Delhi's authority into central India.

Control over these regions improved the Sultanate's strategic position and reduced the power of rival kingdoms. However, the method of administration varied among conquered territories.

Expansion towards the Deccan and southern India

Alauddin had raided Devagiri in 1296 while he was still governor of Kara, before becoming Sultan. This raid must be distinguished from his later southern campaigns as ruler of Delhi.

The most important southern expeditions were conducted under his commander Malik Kafur. These campaigns reached several major kingdoms.

  • Devagiri: An important Yadava political centre in the Deccan, attacked again during Alauddin's reign.
  • Warangal: Capital of the Kakatiya rulers; its ruler accepted Sultanate superiority and agreed to pay tribute following Malik Kafur's campaign in 1310.
  • Dwarasamudra: An important Hoysala centre, reached during the campaign of 1311.
  • Madurai and the Pandya region: Reached by Malik Kafur's expedition during 1311.

Many southern expeditions were intended to secure recognition of Delhi's supremacy and obtain tribute and wealth. They did not necessarily result in the immediate annexation of every conquered kingdom.

For example, the rulers of Warangal and Dwarasamudra agreed to provide tribute rather than having their entire territories immediately incorporated into direct Sultanate administration. This distinction is important when interpreting the extent of Alauddin's empire.

The Mongol threat and military measures

During Alauddin's reign, the Delhi Sultanate faced repeated Mongol invasions. Delhi was threatened in 1299–1300 and again in 1302–1303.

Alauddin maintained a large standing army, meaning soldiers kept in continuous military service rather than assembled only for individual campaigns. He established the fortified military settlement of Siri in Delhi to support his army.

Maintaining such an army required reliable supplies and substantial expenditure. Alauddin therefore introduced measures to improve military supervision and control the cost of essential goods.

Military identification and supervision

Two important terms associated with Alauddin's military administration were:

  • Dagh: Branding of horses to help verify the identity and quality of cavalry animals.
  • Chehra or huliya: Descriptive records of soldiers used for identification and inspection.

These measures helped officials check whether soldiers and horses presented during inspections corresponded to the state's records.

Market regulations and revenue measures

Alauddin paid many soldiers cash salaries. Soldiers needed to purchase food, clothing and other necessities, so rising prices would make it more expensive to maintain a large army.

To control this expenditure, Alauddin regulated prices in Delhi's markets. Officials supervised merchants and attempted to ensure that goods were sold at prescribed prices.

He also strengthened state supervision of land revenue. In the agricultural region between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers, known as the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, the state assessed revenue directly and demanded a substantial share of agricultural produce.

The land-revenue tax called kharaj could amount to approximately 50% of the peasant's produce in areas subject to these measures. This figure should not be interpreted as a uniform rate applicable to every territory throughout the entire Sultanate period.

End of Khalji rule

Alauddin died in 1316. Political instability followed his death. Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah was another important Khalji ruler and governed until 1320.

After the brief seizure of power by Khusrau Khan, Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq overthrew him in 1320 and established the Tughlaq Dynasty.

Prelims focus

  • 1290: Jalaluddin Khalji founded the Khalji Dynasty.
  • 1296–1316: Reign of Alauddin Khalji.
  • 1299: Gujarat expedition led by Ulugh Khan and Nusrat Khan; Anhilwara was sacked.
  • 1301, 1303 and 1305: Ranthambore, Chittor and Malwa respectively.
  • Malik Kafur: Major commander associated with campaigns in the Deccan and southern India.
  • Trap: Alauddin raided Devagiri in 1296 before becoming Sultan; Gujarat in 1299 was his first major territorial expansion campaign as Sultan.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 34–42; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Std 7, Chapter 2, The Delhi Sultanate; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, History, Std 11, Chapter 14, Delhi Sultanate, printed pp. 122–123; IGNOU eGyanKosh, Territorial Expansion, Unit 15, Sections 15.2.1–15.2.3, consulted 19 November 2026.]

title: Khalji Dynasty (1290–1320): Alauddin Khalji and the Expansion of the Sultanate

body:
Establishment of the Tughlaq Dynasty

The Tughlaq Dynasty succeeded the Khaljis in 1320 and continued until 1414. Its period included the greatest territorial reach of Sultanate armies, ambitious administrative experiments and a subsequent decline in central authority.

The major Tughlaq rulers were Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq, Muhammad bin Tughlaq and Firuz Shah Tughlaq.

Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq: Founder of the dynasty

Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq established the dynasty in 1320 after overthrowing Khusrau Khan.

He attempted to restore political stability following the disturbances that ended Khalji rule. He strengthened military authority and worked to recover control over territories whose allegiance to Delhi had weakened.

He is associated with the construction of Tughlaqabad, an important fortified city in the Delhi region.

Military campaigns under Ghiyasuddin and his son helped restore and extend Sultanate authority, including over parts of the eastern and southern territories. His son subsequently became the ruler known as Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

Ghiyasuddin died in 1325 according to commonly used historical chronologies, although some NCERT chronology tables place the transition in 1324. The dynasty's starting year, 1320, is consistent across these accounts.

Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Ambition and administrative experiments

Muhammad bin Tughlaq (approximately 1325–1351) was one of the most distinctive rulers of the Delhi Sultanate.

During the earlier part of his reign, the Sultanate's military and political reach extended across a very large part of the subcontinent. Its territories and campaigns reached from the northwestern frontier towards the Deccan and far southern regions.

However, the size of the territory over which Delhi claimed authority should not be confused with uniform, effective administration. Several distant provinces later rebelled or established independent governments.

Transfer of the capital to Daulatabad

Muhammad bin Tughlaq ordered the transfer of the capital from Delhi to Daulatabad, the former Devagiri, in the Deccan.

Daulatabad's more central location within the expanded territories was an important geographical consideration. The transfer was intended to improve the Sultanate's position in relation to its extensive southern possessions.

The movement of officials and sections of Delhi's population caused considerable hardship and resentment. The policy was subsequently reversed, and Delhi again became the principal capital.

The important distinction is that Daulatabad was a Tughlaq capital-transfer experiment, not a new city founded by Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

Introduction of token currency

Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced a form of token currency using relatively inexpensive metals such as copper and brass.

A token coin has an officially assigned monetary value greater than the intrinsic value of the metal from which it is made. Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted to make these coins circulate at a value comparable to more valuable silver currency.

The experiment encountered serious difficulties because counterfeit coins could be produced relatively easily. People also lacked confidence in the new currency. The Sultan eventually withdrew the token coins.

Iltutmish: Associated with standardising silver tanka and copper jital coinage.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Associated with the unsuccessful experiment of token currency made from inexpensive metals.

Higher taxation in the Ganga-Yamuna Doab

Muhammad bin Tughlaq attempted to raise additional revenue from the Ganga-Yamuna Doab, the fertile region between the Ganga and Yamuna rivers.

The increased demands coincided with famine and agricultural difficulties. The additional burden contributed to widespread discontent and rebellion.

This policy should be distinguished from Alauddin Khalji's earlier efforts to strengthen the regular assessment and collection of land revenue.

Military plans beyond the northwestern frontier

Muhammad bin Tughlaq also planned a major military campaign towards territories beyond the northwestern frontier, including the Khurasan-Transoxiana region. A large army was assembled for the proposed expedition, but the plan was abandoned.

Unlike Alauddin Khalji's predominantly defensive measures against Mongol attacks, Muhammad bin Tughlaq considered an ambitious offensive beyond the Sultanate's established frontiers.

Why did Muhammad bin Tughlaq's policies fail?

The main difficulty was not simply that his plans were unusual. Several measures required effective administration, sufficient resources, public cooperation and reliable control over distant territories.

Their implementation created different problems:

  • Capital transfer: The movement to Daulatabad disrupted established arrangements and caused hardship.
  • Token currency: Easy counterfeiting and weak public confidence undermined circulation.
  • Higher taxation: Increased revenue demands during famine contributed to rebellion.
  • Military expansion plans: Maintaining large forces and preparing distant expeditions placed pressure on state resources.

Firuz Shah Tughlaq: Public works and administration

Firuz Shah Tughlaq (1351–1388) succeeded Muhammad bin Tughlaq.

Firuz Shah is particularly associated with public works, irrigation facilities and the construction of cities. He encouraged canal construction to support agriculture and developed public buildings and other facilities.

He established Firuzabad in the Delhi region and is associated with the foundation of Jaunpur. His reign is also remembered for the relocation of Ashokan pillars to Delhi.

His policies differed from Muhammad bin Tughlaq's ambitious military and currency experiments. Nevertheless, the Sultanate did not recover its earlier effective authority over all distant provinces.

The weakening of the Tughlaq Dynasty

After Firuz Shah's death in 1388, succession conflicts and the growing independence of provincial governors further weakened the Sultanate.

The most destructive external event was the invasion of Timur in 1398. Timur's forces attacked Delhi and caused extensive devastation. The invasion severely damaged the Sultanate's remaining political and military strength.

However, the decline had begun before Timur's invasion. Distant provinces had already challenged Delhi's authority, and important regional kingdoms were emerging.

The Tughlaq Dynasty ended in 1414, when Khizr Khan took control of Delhi and established the Sayyid Dynasty.

Prelims focus

  • 1320: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq founded the Tughlaq Dynasty.
  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Capital-transfer experiment involving Delhi and Daulatabad.
  • Muhammad bin Tughlaq: Introduced token currency that was later withdrawn.
  • Firuz Shah Tughlaq: Ruled from 1351 to 1388; associated with canals and public works.
  • 1398: Timur invaded Delhi during the later Tughlaq period.
  • Trap: The Sultanate reached its widest military and territorial extent under Muhammad bin Tughlaq, but this did not mean that every distant region remained under effective control throughout his reign.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts-II, Class 7, Chapter 3, The Delhi Sultans, printed pp. 35 and 40–42; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, Social Science, Std 7, Chapter 2, The Delhi Sultanate; Gujarat State Board of School Textbooks, History, Std 11, Chapter 14, Delhi Sultanate, printed pp. 123–124; IGNOU eGyanKosh, Territorial Expansion, Unit 15, Section 15.3, consulted 19 November 2026.]
